stem: Which of the following best describes the components that contribute to a child's occipitofrontal circumference (OFC)?

options.text: Brain volume, cerebrospinal fluid, blood, and skull bone thickness
Brain volume and skull thickness only
Grey matter, white matter, and scalp thickness
Brain volume, intracranial pressure, and hair density
Brain volume and cerebrospinal fluid only

explanation: Brain volume, cerebrospinal fluid, blood, and skull bone thickness all contribute to occipitofrontal circumference.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because OFC reflects the size of the intracranial contents as well as the skull, including brain volume, cerebrospinal fluid, blood, and skull bone thickness.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because skull thickness is only one part of the measurement and this option omits cerebrospinal fluid and blood.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because grey and white matter are parts of the brain, but scalp thickness is not a main component of OFC and the option omits cerebrospinal fluid, blood, and skull bone.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because intracranial pressure affects physiology but is not itself a component of OFC, and hair density does not contribute to the measurement.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because OFC includes more than brain volume and cerebrospinal fluid, with blood and skull bone thickness also contributing.

source.hint: Think about all the physical structures and fluids contained within or making up the cranial vault.
